chunks.content: 1 Introduction Autoimmune diseases are typically chronic conditions characterized by a wide range of clinical manifestations affecting multiple organs ( ; ; ; ; ). The pathogenic mechanisms underlying these diseases remain largely unresolved, and they are often incurable. These conditions frequently result in high rates of disability and mortality. The status quo of high medical costs associated with long-term medication use, in addition to the fact that some patients are ineffective or intolerant to conventional medications (antirheumatic drugs, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and glucocorticosteroids) ( ; ), makes the treatment of autoimmune diseases an important clinical issue. It is now well established that B cells play a crucial role in various autoimmune diseases. Several commonly used biologics exert their therapeutic effects by targeting and inhibiting B cell activation or proliferation. For instance, rituximab, an anti-CD20 agent frequently used for B cell-mediated diseases ( ), is costly, necessitates frequent injections, and does not fully deplete B cells to achieve complete remission ( ). Thus, there is a clear need to investigate alternative treatment modalities. CAR-T cell therapy has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in treating leukemia and malignant tumors. Leveraging its therapeutic principle—where CAR-T cells are engineered to target and eliminate pathological immune cells—offers promising insights for its application in autoimmune diseases ( ; ). Several clinical studies of CAR-T for the treatment of autoimmunity have been conducted with encouraging results ( ; ). This article provides an overview of the advancements in utilizing CAR-T therapy for treating autoimmune diseases. Our center has also conducted a clinical trial registered with the NCT for patients with relapsed and refractory systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), where CAR-T therapy has demonstrated promising efficacy in treating autoimmune conditions. 2 Mechanisms underlying CAR-T therapy in autoimmune diseases Pathologic cells associated with autoimmune diseases include autoantibody-producing B cells, activated T cells, and antigen-presenting cells (antigen-presenting cells, APCs) ( ). Among them, B cells are mainly responsible for the humoral immune response and play an important role in a variety of autoimmune diseases by producing antibodies, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines and activating T cells as APCs ( ) ( ). Systemic lupus erythematosus is a complex disease characterized by antibody production and heterogeneity of clinical manifestations, with disruption of B-cell tolerance being a critical early event in the course of the disease ( ; ). Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic, progressive autoimmune disease in which defects in B-cell tolerance checkpoints, autoreactive B cells acting as antigen-presenting cells (APCs) to stimulate the activation of autoreactive T cells, and the production of proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines, are functions that, either individually or in combination, contribute to the pathogenesis of RA (( )). In addition, multiple B cell subpopulations have been found in the salivary glands of patients with desiccation syndrome ( ; ; ; ), and BAFF plays a prominent role in its pathogenesis as an essential survival factor for both transitional and mature B cells ( ). Systemic sclerosis is also a systemic autoimmune disease, mainly characterized by autoimmune abnormalities, especially B cells play an important role in the development of systemic sclerosis. Patients with this disease often present with hypergammaglobulinemia and the presence of various autoantibodies ( ). Anti-synthetase syndrome is a distinct subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, characterized by the presence of autoantibodies—particularly anti-Jo-1 antibodies—which are frequently associated with pathological manifestations such as interstitial lung disease, Raynaud’s phenomenon, and arthritis. Given these associations, deep depletion of B cells may offer therapeutic benefits. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a life-threatening systemic autoimmune disease, driven by autoantigens such as myeloperoxidase (MPO) or protease 3. Therapeutic strategies have been explored to achieve clinical benefits by depleting B cells that produce MPO-ANCA(( )) ( ). Current treatments for autoimmune diseases focus on suppressing the immune system through small molecules that inhibit immune cell activation or proliferation, such as the B-cell depleting drug anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody rituximab, which was initially approved for use in certain types of B-cell malignancies and is now used to treat B-cell mediated autoimmune disease. However, some patients do not show remission, and even when effective, frequent injections are required and there is a risk of chronic B-cell failure and infection due to chronic immunosuppression ( ). The drug has also been found to struggle with the complete elimination of B cells, as evidenced by the persistence of B cells within the synovium of rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with rituximab. This suggests that tissue-resident B cells may evade depletion by rituximab, in contrast to circulating B cells ( ). Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) immunotherapy is a novel therapeutic approach that involves the extraction of T cells, either autologous or allogeneic, followed by in vitro expansion and subsequent infusion into the patient ( ). Genetic material with specific antigen recognition domains and T-cell activation signals are transferred into T cells

also been found to struggle with the complete elimination of B cells, as evidenced by the persistence of B cells within the synovium of rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with rituximab. This suggests that tissue-resident B cells may evade depletion by rituximab, in contrast to circulating B cells ( ). Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) immunotherapy is a novel therapeutic approach that involves the extraction of T cells, either autologous or allogeneic, followed by in vitro expansion and subsequent infusion into the patient ( ). Genetic material with specific antigen recognition domains and T-cell activation signals are transferred into T cells by retroviruses or lentiviruses, so that T cells no longer require APCs for activation, and these CAR-T cells initially bind to antigen-expressing target cells and subsequently exert their cytotoxic effects, leading to the lysis of the target cells. In addition, CAR-T cells can differentiate into long-lived memory cells in vivo , facilitating more sustained remission. Leveraging the cytotoxicity and tissue infiltration capabilities of T cells, CAR-T cells can also effectively target difficult-to-reach, tissue-resident tumor cells. In comparison, conventional drugs are ineffective or intolerable for many patients, and biologic anti-cd20 antibodies require repeated administration to maintain therapy ( ). And over time, the host can become resistant to treatment, all of which further limits the use of conventional drugs. A classic CAR has three main portions: ecto-domain, transmembrane domain and endo-domain. The ecto-domain includes a recognition domain of the antigen and a hinge domain, and the endodomain is characterized as a costimulatory and intracellular signaling domain. The first generation of CARs only consisted of three simple parts, there was no co-stimulation part, which could not secrete enough cytokines and led to the failure of amplification. Therefore, co-stimulation signals were added on the basis of the first generation, and the second generation of CARs was born. The co-stimulation signal can induce the proliferation of T cells and the release of cellular factors. The subsequent generations were designed on the basis of the second generation, the third generation added a stimulating factor on the basis of the second generation, and the fourth and fifth generations added cytokines to regulate the tumor microenvironment to enhance efficacy ( ) ( ; ; ). 3 Classification of CARs 3.1 Classification of CARs according to their cell type CAR-T cells are genetically engineered T cells designed to express synthetic receptors on their surface, enabling them to identify and eliminate cancer cells by recognizing specific tumor antigens independently of human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules ( ). Initially conceived as a “living drug” to target and destroy tumors, CAR-T cells have shown promising efficacy in this regard. Natural killer (NK) cells eliminate target cells through two primary mechanisms: the release of cytolytic granules and the induction of apoptosis via Fas ligand (FasL). The incorporation of chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) enables both T cells and natural killer (NK) cells to selectively and effectively target and eliminate cancer cells. And it was observed that CAR NK has a better safety profile ( ). It also paves the way for the development of off-the-shelf CAR products that can be cryopreserved for long-term storage ( ). However, CAR-NK cells suffer from limited durability. A significant challenge for both CAR-T and CAR-NK cells in the treatment of solid tumors is their difficulty in effectively infiltrating the tumor’s interior. So researchers began introducing CARs into macrophages, which are able to infiltrate solid tumors naturally and effectively ( ; ; ). To overcome these drawbacks, other cell therapies are being developed, and currently there are NK cells, macrophages, Treg cells, neutrophils, and pluripotent stem cell-derived CARs cell therapies ( ). 3.2 Classification according to target CD19 is a surface antigen predominantly expressed on B-lineage malignancies. It has become a prominent target for CAR-T therapy, beginning with the approval of Kymriah as the first anti-CD19 CAR product in 2017. Since then, CD19 CAR-T therapy has demonstrated success in clinical trials across various B-cell cancers ( ; ). And gradually more targets such as BCMA, CD22, CD7, CD20, etc., have also been introduced in order to deeply deplete B cells ( ). 3.3 Classification according to the source of CAR-T and the mode of infusion The manufacturing process for autologous CAR-T cells takes approximately 3 weeks, during which patients may experience disease progression. To address this issue, universal CAR-T cells derived from allogeneic sources have been proposed as an alternative. It is expected to be produced on a large scale as an “off-the-shelf” drug. Recently, Wang et al. reported the first use of allogeneic CAR-T cells in patients with autoimmune diseases. All three patients showed significant clinical improvement. And they showed significant clinical improvement and remained in remission for the 6 months of follow-up to date ( ; ). A major adverse event of allogeneic CAR-T therapy

process for autologous CAR-T cells takes approximately 3 weeks, during which patients may experience disease progression. To address this issue, universal CAR-T cells derived from allogeneic sources have been proposed as an alternative. It is expected to be produced on a large scale as an “off-the-shelf” drug. Recently, Wang et al. reported the first use of allogeneic CAR-T cells in patients with autoimmune diseases. All three patients showed significant clinical improvement. And they showed significant clinical improvement and remained in remission for the 6 months of follow-up to date ( ; ). A major adverse event of allogeneic CAR-T therapy is the risk of GvHD due to attack of host organs by the injected T cells. No signs of GvHD have been reported in these patients, and another important safety issue in CAR-T therapy is CRS. However, Wang et al. did not observe any clinical signs of severe CRS. This may be due to the fact that the target burden of autoimmune diseases is much smaller compared to cancer. Alternatively, new approaches are being explored to eliminate in vitro manufacturing time through gene editing, namely in vivo cell reprogramming for in situ cell therapy ( ). Currently, in situ reprogramming of target cells includes both viral and non-viral approaches. Viral vectors can mediate effective delivery, but are accompanied by immunogenicity and safety issues. Synthetic nanomaterials, such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which have smaller immunogenicity, are easy to produce and low-cost, are promising alternatives to viral vectors, although they are still in the initial stages of exploration ( ). 4 Advances in CAR⁃T therapy for autoimmune diseases 4.1 CAR-T for systemic lupus erythematosus Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a highly heterogeneous autoimmune disease that affects almost all organs and tissues ( ). Disruption of immune tolerance and persistent autoantibody production are the two main features of SLE. Current CAR-T cell therapy targets for the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) include CD19, CD20, and BCMA. Administering anti-CD19 CAR-T cells in a mouse model of severe lupus nephritis led to improved disease outcomes and prolonged lifespan, indicating the efficacy of this therapy in SLE and underscoring its potential for clinical application ( ). Elevated numbers of follicular helper CD4 + T cells (TFH) have been observed in patients with SLE, particularly during disease flares, with TFH counts correlating with levels of programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) expression ( ). Seth D. Reighard et al. designed and evaluated an innovative CAR-NK cell that targets PD-1-expressing cells to eliminate TFH. In short-term in vitro co-cultures, these PD-1-targeting CAR-NK cells selectively cleared TFH cells. These results bring new ideas for the treatment of SLE (( )). CAR Treg cells theoretically hold promise for restoring Treg numbers and function as a treatment for SLE. However, IL-21 secreted by CD4 + T cells compromises Treg survival and function, and a highly pro-inflammatory environment can drive Treg cells to convert into IL-17-producing or other inflammatory factor-secreting cells. These challenges underscore the complexities of using CAR Treg cells in SLE treatment, necessitating further investigation ( ). So far, 25cases of SLE treated with CAR-T have been reported, including 10cases in Germany ( ), 10 cases in China, and five cases in the US [( )]. In August 2021, Georgschett’s team reported the first patient treated with CAR-T for systemic lupus erythematosus, in which dsDNA autoantibody titers and C3 and C4 complement levels returned to normal after 5 weeks of CAR-T cell injections, proteinuria was virtually eradicated, and the Disease Activity Index was reduced from a score of 16 to 0, with no significant side effects ( ). The team later reported on nine additional lupus patients treated with CAR-T, all of whom improved significantly ( ; ; ; ). Our center has also conducted a clinical study of CD19 CAR-T for the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus ( NCT06056921 ), which has been administered to two patients, both of whom have demonstrated improvement and a favorable safety profile. 4.2 CAR-T for Sjögre’s syndrome Sjögre’s syndrome (SS) is a chronic autoimmune disease with multiple manifestations, the main manifestations of which include dryness of the mouth and eyes, as well as systemic complications ( ). B-cell overactivity is evidenced by the presence of various autoantibodies, including RF and anti-SSA/SSB antibodies, as well as by hypergammaglobulinemia. Additionally, some patients with systemic sclerosis may develop malignant B-cell lymphomas. B-cell activating factor (BAFF) is a key driver of systemic sclerosis (SS) development, playing a crucial role in promoting B-cell survival and hyperactivity ( ). Certain targeted therapies, such as rituximab, exert their therapeutic effects by depleting B cells. Anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy is similar in principle to CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy, which also treats SS through B-cell depletion. However, it has been observed that long-lived plasma cells in many SS patients do not

the presence of various autoantibodies, including RF and anti-SSA/SSB antibodies, as well as by hypergammaglobulinemia. Additionally, some patients with systemic sclerosis may develop malignant B-cell lymphomas. B-cell activating factor (BAFF) is a key driver of systemic sclerosis (SS) development, playing a crucial role in promoting B-cell survival and hyperactivity ( ). Certain targeted therapies, such as rituximab, exert their therapeutic effects by depleting B cells. Anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy is similar in principle to CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy, which also treats SS through B-cell depletion. However, it has been observed that long-lived plasma cells in many SS patients do not express or express very low levels of CD20, and thus CD20 monoclonal antibodies cannot target them. In contrast to CD20, which is expressed primarily on mature B cells, CD19 is widely expressed throughout the maturation process of pre-B cells into plasma cells. This broader expression profile suggests that CD19 may be a more effective target for immunotherapy. Currently, two Phase I studies ( NCT05085431 and NCT05859997 ) are investigating the safety and efficacy of CD19/BCMA CAR-T cells for the treatment of systemic sclerosis. The results of these studies have yet to be reported. To date, only a single case has been reported from Germany, involving a patient with a 10-year history of dry syndrome and secondary interstitial lung disease, who was subsequently diagnosed with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma ( ). Following treatment with anti-CD19 CAR-T cells, the patient achieved complete remission (CR). Notably, by day 90 post-therapy, the patient tested negative for antinuclear antibodies and anti-Ro-52 for the first time. Early in the treatment, the patient exhibited grade 2 cytokine release syndrome and grade 1 neurotoxicity, but the adverse effects were completely controlled after aggressive treatment, proving that they were tolerated reasonably well. As for more long-term efficacy, long-term follow-up is needed to confirm this. 4.3 CAR-T for systemic sclerosis Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a connective tissue disease marked by autoimmunity, vasculopathy, excessive extracellular matrix deposition, and fibrosis, leading to atrophy of the skin, subcutaneous tissues, muscles, and internal organs, including the digestive system, lungs, heart, kidneys, and central nervous system ( ). Multiple lines of evidence suggest that B cells play a significant role in the pathophysiology of severe systemic sclerosis. And CD19 was found to be significantly increased in expression in memory B cells and naive B cells in SSc ( ), so the current target of CAR-T clinical trials for the treatment of SSc is CD19. The efficacy of the CD20 antibody-targeted drug rituximab (RTX) in the treatment of SSc remains controversial, with the use of rituximab demonstrating significant skin improvement in one randomized controlled trial, but it led to a decrease in forceful lung capacity (FVC) in another study ( ). Changes in Treg populations were also observed in SSc patients, with a disruption of the balance between Treg and Th17 cells, an immune imbalance that has been implicated as a cause of the disease ( ; ). As potential treatments for systemic sclerosis (SSc), therapies targeting Treg or Th17 cells are being explored with the aim of restoring the balance between these cell types ( ). In systemic sclerosis (SSc), myelin basic protein (MBP) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) can act as potential targets within the central nervous system (CNS). Human Tregs have been designed to express the Ob2F3 TCR V region to target myelin basic protein (MBP), and experiments suggest that these ob2f3-expressing Treg cells ameliorate experimental autoimmune encephalitis in transgenic mice ( ). These significant findings indicate that engineered CAR-Tregs targeting the CNS have the potential to be developed for cellular therapy in patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc). Reports have documented six cases of systemic sclerosis treated with CAR-T therapy, all originating from Germany ( ; ; ; ). After CAR-T cell infusion, none of them experienced serious adverse effects, only mild cytokine release syndrome (CRS) grade 1, no signs of neurotoxicity, and all of them demonstrated autoantibody turnaround and rapid improvement of multisystemic manifestations of cardiac, joint, and cutaneous involvement in subsequent short-term follow-up, these data offer the initial evidence that targeted CD19 CAR-T cell therapy may be effective in treating severe cases of systemic sclerosis ( ), but they do not fully clarify whether it is only a short-term effect of CAR-T cell therapy, and further observation of the extent of drug-free remission in SSc is warranted. 4.4 CAR-T for idiopathic inflammatory myopathies Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) are a heterogeneous group of autoimmune disorders. Muscle weakness is usually the typical clinical presentation, but other organs may also be affected, including the skin, joints, lungs, heart, etc. Different myositis-specific auto-antibodies have been identified and IIM can be classified into several subgroups - dermatomyositis (including amyopathic dermatomyositis), antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, inclusion body myositis, polymyositis and overlap myositis ( ). According to

Muscle weakness is usually the typical clinical presentation, but other organs may also be affected, including the skin, joints, lungs, heart, etc. Different myositis-specific auto-antibodies have been identified and IIM can be classified into several subgroups - dermatomyositis (including amyopathic dermatomyositis), antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, inclusion body myositis, polymyositis and overlap myositis ( ). According to its pathogenesis, B-cell depletion shows promise in controlling the progression of the disease. Four patients with antisynthetase syndrome treated with CAR-T have been reported and all have shown favorable outcomes ( ; ). Three of them developed low-grade CRS, including one with ICANS, and symptoms improved with tolizumab treatment. Longer-term follow-up and additional clinical trials are needed to assess the longer-term therapeutic profile of CAR-T in antisynthetase syndrome. 4.5 CAR-T for ANCA-associated vasculitis ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) encompasses a group of systemic autoimmune disorders marked by inflammation of small blood vessels and endothelial dysfunction. This condition can impact various organs and tissues, including the skin, lungs, kidneys, heart, gastrointestinal tract, and central nervous system. Based on clinical features and pathological manifestations, ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) can be categorized into three subgroups: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) ( ). The pathogenesis of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) remains not fully elucidated. However, Lodka et al. have demonstrated the feasibility and efficacy of CD19 CAR-T cell therapy for AAV treatment using a mouse model of MPO-AAV. Although myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA was not completely eliminated, its levels were significantly reduced and demonstrated a strong protective effect against autoantibody-induced glomerulonephritis ( ). The application of this therapy for ANCA-associated vasculitis is currently restricted to vivo studies, and further data are needed to confirm its safety and efficacy. 4.6 CAR-T for rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, inflammatory, systemic autoimmune disease that affects the joints with severity that varies from patient to patient ( ), with risk factors including age, gender, genetics, and environmental exposures (smoking, air pollutants, and occupation). RA is presently incurable, and the goal of treatment is to reduce pain and stop or slow further damage. The pathogenesis and etiology of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain largely unknown. However, protein citrullination has long been identified as a key feature that triggers the immune response associated with this condition. The presence of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) in serum is one of the most specific serological markers for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and is closely linked to the disease’s development ( ; ). Previous studies have shown that RA patients are significantly heterogeneous and different patients can exhibit different types of autoantibodies. Zhang et al. demonstrated that anti-FITC CAR-Ts can be specifically targeted to tumor cells or autoreactive B cells of RA patients with high levels of autoantibodies by citrullinated peptide epitopes labeled with FITC (fluorescein isothiocyanate), and that this approach can be used according to the individual characteristics of a given RA patient to eliminate the respective specific subpopulation of autoreactive cells. This opens up a new field of targeted therapy for autoimmune diseases ( ). However, the main limitation of this study is that it only demonstrated that it is possible to eliminate auto-reactive B cells in vitro and lacks evidence of therapeutic efficacy in vivo . Therefore, its feasibility and safety in vivo are unknown and need to be further explored in a large number of experiments. In addition, citrullinated waveform protein (CV) has been identified as a specific antigen found exclusively in the extracellular matrix of inflamed synovial tissues in RA patients and has been suggested as a potential target for CAR-T cell therapy ( ). Preliminary data suggest that CAR-Tregs targeting citrullinated waveform protein (CV) may play a role in RA, but preclinical manifestations are not yet clear ( ). 5 Current clinical trials A search of clinicaltrials.gov was performed for currently ongoing clinical trials of CAR-T for the treatment of SLE, SS, SSc, AAV, and RA. (Search date 2024.7.15, with no results found for ASS) ( ). 6 Challenges and strategies for CAR-T treatment of autoimmune diseases While CAR-T therapy has demonstrated significant efficacy in treating both hematologic and solid tumors, it continues to encounter several challenges ( ). 6.1 Pre-infusion 6.1.1 CAR-T manufacturing is time-consuming Autologous CAR-T cell therapy involves a highly complex process of customizing CAR-T cells following the isolation of each patient’s white blood cells. This procedure typically requires approximately 3 weeks to complete ( ; ). In response to the problem of long in vitro manufacturing time, universal CAR-T (UCAR-T) has been proposed, which is taken from T cells of healthy

( ). 6 Challenges and strategies for CAR-T treatment of autoimmune diseases While CAR-T therapy has demonstrated significant efficacy in treating both hematologic and solid tumors, it continues to encounter several challenges ( ). 6.1 Pre-infusion 6.1.1 CAR-T manufacturing is time-consuming Autologous CAR-T cell therapy involves a highly complex process of customizing CAR-T cells following the isolation of each patient’s white blood cells. This procedure typically requires approximately 3 weeks to complete ( ; ). In response to the problem of long in vitro manufacturing time, universal CAR-T (UCAR-T) has been proposed, which is taken from T cells of healthy donors, exempted from the action of heterologous reactive T cells by knocking out genes such as TCR, CD52, CD7, etc., and can be infused back in the spot without waiting, and the large-scale production can significantly reduce the price, which greatly improves the accessibility of CAR-T products ( ), and this approach is expected to break the dilemma. 6.1.2 Disease activity During the time that autologous CAR-T is being manufactured in vitro , a number of patients will experience disease activity as a result of discontinuation of the drug and thus become ineligible for treatment. It may be possible to continue maintenance therapy with low-dose drugs during this period, and in addition, cyclophosphamide and fudarabine, which are used to clear lymphocytes, may have some therapeutic effect [( ; )]. 6.1.3 Poor quality of T cells Immune cells from healthy donors are usually unaffected by cancer effects or exposure to drugs, whereas in tumor patients, which may be related to immunosuppression, the tumor microenvironment, or having undergone multiple lines of therapy, T-cell dysfunction has been observed in tumor patients in the past, and these aberrant T-cells may affect the efficacy of CAR-T therapy ( ; ). Given that patients with autoimmune diseases are frequently treated with glucocorticoids and other medications such as mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide, which can impact the quality and quantity of T cells, it is crucial to consider these factors when evaluating CAR-T therapy ( ). In a clinical study involving CAR-T therapy for five patients with severe, treatment-resistant systemic lupus erythematosus, stable and reproducible production of CD19CAR-T cells from peripheral blood was successfully achieved. This outcome occurred despite the patients having been pre-treated with T-cell-targeting medications, including mycophenolate mofetil and glucocorticoids, as part of their disease management ( ). 6.1.4 High price The high cost of CAR-T therapy is a significant barrier for many patients ( ), largely due to the complexity of the manufacturing process, which involves genetically modifying T cells, tailoring the treatment to each patient, implementing stringent quality-control measures, and requiring specialized facilities for cell production and processing ( ; ). Back in 2017, there were two approved CAR-T drugs available in the United States: Kymriah and Yescarta. Kymriah has a listed price of US$475,000 and Yescarta has a listed price of US$373,000, and that doesn't even include the cost of possible side effects of the treatment, which is why it's currently only used to treat patients with particularly severe autoimmune diseases. Ideally, however, if long-term drug-free remission can be achieved with CAR-T therapy, the cost may be balanced against the cost of long-term repeated use of hormones, immunosuppressants, and biologics to control the disease. In addition to UCAR-T mentioned above, in situ cellular reprogramming, a potentially groundbreaking technology, also opens up possibilities to reduce costs and simplify the acquisition process ( ). It targets and reprograms T cells in vivo to express CARs without the need for any in vitro manufacturing, thus greatly reducing costs, simplifying the acquisition process, and increasing availability. T-cell-targeted mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have recently been found to deliver in vivo coding in mice, allowing the generation of functional CAR-T cells in vivo . . This study demonstrated that a single injection of an off-the-shelf product can effectively reprogram the immune system, a technology that takes CAR-T cell therapy another step toward reducing costs and increasing accessibility. 6.2 Post-infusion 6.2.1 Cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity Although autoimmune diseases can be severe enough to cause death, the mortality rate is significantly lower than that of patients with malignant hematologic tumors. Therefore, the safety of the new treatment modality is the most concerned point for patients and doctors besides the efficacy. After the administration of CAR-T cells, their recognition of target cells triggers activation and proliferation, leading to the destruction of these target cells and the release of various cytokines, including IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-10. The released cytokines further activate the patient’s immune cells, including T cells, B cells, monocytes, and macrophages, as well as non-immune cells such as endothelial cells. After the administration of CAR-T cells, their recognition of target cells triggers activation and proliferation, leading to the destruction of these target cells and the release of various cytokines, including IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-10. The released cytokines further activate the patient’s immune cells, including T cells, B cells, monocytes, and macrophages, as well as non-immune cells such as endothelial cells. This cascade results in the release of additional cytokines, establishing a positive feedback loop known as cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which can escalate into a systemic inflammatory response with the potential to cause significant tissue and organ damage. Experiments have demonstrated that IL-6 plays a pivotal role in mediating cytokine release syndrome (CRS) ( ; ; ). The incidence of CRS is notably high in clinical trials targeting hematologic malignancies ( ; ). However, in CAR-T cell therapy trials for autoimmune diseases, no reports of grade 3 or higher CRS have been observed ( ). The good tolerability of CAR-T cell therapy in autoimmune diseases may be due to the fact that the amount of b-cells in patients with autoimmune diseases is many times lower than in patients with tumors. Therefore, cells carrying the target antigen (CD19) are quickly removed. Additionally, some patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia experience severe neurotoxicity, referred to as immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), following CAR-T cell therapy ( ). However, in the limited number of patients with autoimmune diseases currently undergoing CAR-T cell therapy, we have observed a relatively favorable tolerability profile, with no serious adverse effects reported ( ). Although some patients experienced a mild cytokine storm, this was effectively managed with prompt symptomatic treatment and tolizumab administration. 6.2.2 Hematotoxicity Hematotoxicity, which includes manifestations such as anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia ( ), may occur early due to lymphocyte depletion before CAR-T therapy. Its late onset, however, is often associated with the severity of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) during treatment. This phenomenon has been observed in the management of both oncological and autoimmune diseases ( ). Therefore, we need to closely monitor the changes in blood routine during the treatment period, and promptly transfuse component blood when necessary. 6.2.3 Off-target Off-target effects, where CAR-T cells either cross-react with non-target molecules or target antigens expressed on normal cells, are more commonly observed in tumor therapies ( ; ). These phenomena have not been reported in clinical trials of CAR-T therapy for autoimmune diseases. However, careful monitoring is essential to detect their potential occurrence during treatment. 6.2.4 Infection Patients undergoing CAR-T cell therapy face an elevated risk of infection due to several factors, including immunodeficiency from their underlying disease, prior cytotoxic treatments, lymphodepleting therapy, potential complications such as CRS and ICANS, as well as neutropenia and hypogammaglobulinemia. Infectious complications, both early and late, are commonly observed following CAR-T cell administration in the treatment of hematologic malignancies ( ). However, such complications have not been specifically reported in the context of autoimmune diseases. Evidence-based guidelines for anti-infective prophylaxis following CAR-T cell therapy are lacking, and routine use of fungal and bacterial prophylaxis is uncommon. However, it should be actively considered in patients with neutropenia. 6.3 Long-term mitigation 6.3.1 Recurring A critical feature of CAR-T therapy is its capacity to identify target antigens and exert cytotoxic effects. When B cells proliferate again it may lead to disease relapse. However, a recent study found that after CAR-T treatment for autoimmune disease, newly emerged B cells predominantly expressed IgM and IgD, while memory B cells and plasmablasts were nearly absent. IgD is often expressed in relatively naïve B cells, including naïve B cells (IgD + CD27 − ), unswitched memory B cells (IgD+CD27 + ), So the phenomenon may be related to inflammatory suppression, deep B-cell clearance and subsequent reconstitution. ( ; ). 6.3.2 Secondary tumors CAR transgenes are integrated into the genome of T cells primarily through viruses, a process that may lead to tumors. Secondary malignancies have been reported after CAR T-cell therapy, including myelodysplastic syndromes, bladder cancer, or nonmelanoma skin cancers ( ; ), therefore, there have been attempts to use vectors and gene editing techniques other than retroviruses and lentiviruses to create a safer product, with adeno-associated viruses and targeted nucleases offering promise ( ). 6.3.3 B-cell dysplasia Current clinical trials using CAR-T therapies have focused on removing B-cell markers such as CD19 or BCMA, and prolonged low levels of B-cells are often observed after CAR-T treatment of blood disorders, leaving patients susceptible to symptoms such as infections ( ), and targeting infections that occur as a result of this B-cell dysplasia can be achieved with intravenous immune globulin. However, this has not been observed in autoimmune diseases for the moment ( ) ( ). This regeneration of B cells is also a major

product, with adeno-associated viruses and targeted nucleases offering promise ( ). 6.3.3 B-cell dysplasia Current clinical trials using CAR-T therapies have focused on removing B-cell markers such as CD19 or BCMA, and prolonged low levels of B-cells are often observed after CAR-T treatment of blood disorders, leaving patients susceptible to symptoms such as infections ( ), and targeting infections that occur as a result of this B-cell dysplasia can be achieved with intravenous immune globulin. However, this has not been observed in autoimmune diseases for the moment ( ) ( ). This regeneration of B cells is also a major point of difference in comparison to CAR-T therapy for tumors, the mechanism of which is currently unclear. Possible reasons for this include the fact that, unlike cancer patients, patients with autoimmune diseases receive fewer cytotoxic drugs, so stem cells and immune cells may be less affected ( ). This may also be related to the distinct cellular niches for memory. CAR T cells. The location of memory CAR-T cells is importantly linked to their persistence and B-cell reset. The earlier appearance of B-cell proliferation in lupus patients may be due to the fact that CAR T cells are located in secondary lymphoid organs, whereas in leukaemia memory CAR T cells are located in the bone marrow ( ). However, the proliferation of B-cells is theoretically incompatible with the long-term efficacy of CAR-t therapy, so a large number of clinical trials are needed to assess the long-term efficacy of CAR-T in autoimmune diseases. 7 Conclusion As mentioned above, CAR-T has been explored for the treatment of a variety of autoimmune diseases, with current clinical trials showing good efficacy and a fair safety profile compared to tumors. However, there are some challenges that we need to continue to work to overcome before, during and after its treatment. 8 Future prosepects CAR-T therapy has shown remarkable success in the treatment of hematological diseases and solid tumors, and as an emerging therapy in autoimmune diseases, it has also demonstrated certain potential. However, the number of patients with autoimmune diseases who have received this therapy is not large enough, the follow-up period is short, and the relevant clinical data are still scarce. So the longer-term efficacy and safety are still unclear. We expect that it will become a mature therapy for autoimmune diseases in the future. 9 Method We searched PubMed and Web of science for articles published from From 1 January 2010 to 30 September 2024, using the search terms ‘CAR T cell’ and ‘autoimmune disease’ or ‘Rheumatic Autoimmune Disease’. We also searched for articles linked to the terms ‘B cell depletion’. We restricted our search to articles published in English. We included clinical studies, mechanistic studies, case reports, and case series, as well as reviews on CAR T-cell therapy into our references. Articles related to autologous and allogenic stem cell transplantation in autoimmune diseases, were also included.

Background Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a therapeutic procedure that replaces a patient’s original pathological hematopoietic stem cells with healthy ones to restore hematopoietic and immune functions [ ]. It is the most effective treatment for malignant hematological diseases, severe bone marrow failure, and certain solid tumors [ ]. Between 1957 and 2019, the estimated number of allogeneic HSCT and autologous HSCT procedures performed worldwide exceeded 1.5 million [ ]. HSCT improves overall and disease-free survival in many patients with malignant and nonmalignant hematological diseases [ ]. However, owing to regimen conditioning, a protective isolation environment, lengthy treatment procedures, and high transplantation costs, the burden of HSCT represents a significant challenge for patients [ , ]. Patients typically experience a variety of physical symptoms, such as nausea, vomiting, and oral mucositis, as well as varying degrees of psychological problems, such as anxiety and fear [ , ]. Patients may experience distress due to their inability to tolerate the physical symptoms arising from HSCT. Consequently, restricting patients’ access to potential sources of support can be perceived as an obstacle that undermines their positivity, which may exacerbate physical discomfort [ , ]. This dual impact on physical and mental well-being can create a vicious cycle, ultimately undermining confidence and the capacity for self-management [ ]. Symptom burden can have a significant negative impact on an individual’s physical, psychological, social, and spiritual well-being [ ]. Currently, patients in laminar flow cleanrooms rely primarily on the support of healthcare providers (HCPs). Serving as the only point of contact with patients during isolation, HCPs are responsible for providing specialized clinical care, conveying essential health information, continuously assessing patient conditions, administering timely interventions if symptoms or complications occur, and ensuring daily care. However, the current clinical reality demonstrates the difficulty in meeting each patient’s individualized 24/7 symptom management needs and capturing subtle changes in real time [ ]. Evidence suggests a relationship between reduced symptom burden and effective self-management [ ]. Symptom self-management is defined as a dynamic, self-directed process in which individuals implement behaviors aimed at identifying, preventing, alleviating, or reducing the incidence, frequency, duration, intensity, and degree of distress, complications, and unpleasant emotions associated with symptoms, all of which help to achieve optimal body function [ ]. Active self-management, as the patient is the first person to perceive symptoms, is key to achieving early recognition and timely response. However, several studies have highlighted that the current state of symptom self-management remains unsatisfactory [ , ]. Many patients experience internal predicaments when managing their symptoms owing to a lack of information, symptom coping skills, and inadequate symptom perception [ ]. In addition, patients who are inexperienced or unfamiliar with self-management strategies, particularly those receiving treatment for the first time, may experience negative emotions, such as anxiety and fear, and a sense of losing control over their health [ ]. In contrast to other HSCT contexts, patients in isolation settings are restricted from direct contact with family members. The previous model, in which family members shouldered the primary caregiving responsibilities, has been disrupted, leading to the absence of key care roles [ ]. Familial involvement may increase the patients’ motivation in self-management [ ]. Patients engaged in family caregiving demonstrated greater adherence to self-management programmes than those who were not, suggesting that a lack of such involvement can be a detrimental factor [ ]. This highlights the urgent need to develop and implement effective symptom self-management interventions. Therefore, it is imperative to explore the requirement for self-management of symptoms in this population. The morbidity and distress caused by HSCT-related symptoms can result in various demands [ ]. While the current research highlights the significance of symptom self-management for HSCT patients [ , ], it rarely addresses the specific needs of these patients, particularly those within laminar airflow rooms. Gaining a comprehensive understanding of these needs is crucial to guide the design and implementation of effective symptom management in HSCT patients. Methods Study design A descriptive qualitative study was conducted from October 2023 to January 2024 using semi-structured face-to-face interviews. Symptom management theory (SMT) consists of three core concepts: symptom experience, components of symptom management strategies, and outcomes [ ]. This theory can serve as a guide to explore symptom experiences, evaluate management strategies, and measure adverse outcomes. Therefore, we used SMT for the qualitative study design, which also served as an interview guide for this study. We adopted descriptive qualitative methods to explore symptom self-management strategies, aiming to identify the barriers and needs for symptom self-management in adult patients with HSCT within laminar airflow rooms. We used the SMT as the theoretical framework, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist [ ]. Setting and participants We recruited participants from a HSCT center of a large

guide to explore symptom experiences, evaluate management strategies, and measure adverse outcomes. Therefore, we used SMT for the qualitative study design, which also served as an interview guide for this study. We adopted descriptive qualitative methods to explore symptom self-management strategies, aiming to identify the barriers and needs for symptom self-management in adult patients with HSCT within laminar airflow rooms. We used the SMT as the theoretical framework, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist [ ]. Setting and participants We recruited participants from a HSCT center of a large tertiary hospital in Fujian Province, China. The HSCT center is the largest transplant center in Fujian Province, with 32 single-bed transplant wards. The HSCT ward is an unaccompanied laminar airflow room where family members and caregivers are not allowed to enter. The protective isolation protocol at this center established a standardized clinical pathway and a highly controlled care environment. Patients were confined to laminar airflow rooms continuously from the initiation of conditioning phase until hematopoietic engraftment. Their daily care was facilitated by a dedicated nursing team with a nurse-to-patient ratio of approximately 1:1.5, integrated with daily ward rounds. As visitors were not permitted, patients’ only source of human contact was with staff, who completed a rigorous sequence of hand disinfection, sterile gowning and mask fitting upon entering the room. Within the cultural context of China, where family members are typically deeply involved in hands-on care and daily support, the isolation protocol redirected all immediate, in-person dependencies for daily needs and problem-solving exclusively to HCPs. Purposive sampling was conducted for participant recruitment and data collection from October 2023 to January 2024. Inclusion criteria were (a) 18 years old and above; (b) undergoing HSCT for the first time; (c) were aware of their diagnosis and prognosis; and (d) able to communicate fluently in Mandarin. The exclusion criterion was a current or past mental illness. Maximum variation sampling was used to recruit a heterogeneous sample of patients according to age, sex, education, marital status, type of HSCT, donor source and disease diagnosis. All participants were recruited face-to-face by a researcher, QHC. Initially, the researchers reviewed the patients’ medical records for sociodemographic and disease characteristics. Next, we established contact with the patients, explained the purpose and content of the study, and obtained written informed consent. Data collection To further adjust and refine the draft interview guide, the female researcher, QHC, purposively selected two eligible patients for a pre-interview, modified the interview guide based on their feedback, and developed the final interview guide (Table ). Each interview was conducted by QHC to ensure consistency. Prior to the interviews, the interviewer systematically conducted in-depth theoretical studies of the relevant research and was mentored by a professor with extensive experience in qualitative research. The interviews were in-depth, one-on-one, and took place in a single transplant ward, with no other people present. The interview time was usually between 15:30 and 16:30 or between 18:30 and 20:00 to avoid the time when the patient was undergoing treatment, resting, or eating. All interviews were audio-recorded, and the interviewees’ facial expressions and body language were recorded. When no new codes were extracted, the data were considered saturated, and another patient was interviewed to determine data collection saturation. Data analysis Data collection and preliminary analysis were conducted concurrently and data collection ended when data saturation was reached. Demographic data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 26.0. Two researchers, QHC and JYC, verified the accuracy of the transcribed text before analysis, and the recordings were professionally transcribed within 48 h. Content analysis methods were used to analyze the qualitative data [ ]. Two researchers with experience in HSCT, including one doctoral nursing researcher, JYC, and one master of nursing researcher, QHC, analyzed the data to reduce subjectivity. The data were encoded using NVivo (release 1.2, QSR). Throughout the interview process, field notes were taken to capture contextual information, non-verbal cues, and reflections, which were analyzed alongside the transcribed texts to enrich the data interpretation. First, researchers independently listened to the audio recordings multiple times to gain a clear understanding of the content and then carefully reviewed each interview transcript to conduct the coding process. During the coding and thematic analysis, particular attention was paid to potential variations in experiences based on participants’ disease diagnoses. Final themes and subthemes were developed through discussions between the two researchers. In the case of any disagreements regarding the extracted themes, an experienced nursing professor, RH, was consulted to determine the most appropriate theme. This process ensured the rigor and validity of the findings. Rigor Multiple strategies were used to ensure rigor. First, to ensure a representative sample, sampling strategies considered the participants’ age, sex, marital status, education, and transplant type. Second, to ensure credibility and reduce

Final themes and subthemes were developed through discussions between the two researchers. In the case of any disagreements regarding the extracted themes, an experienced nursing professor, RH, was consulted to determine the most appropriate theme. This process ensured the rigor and validity of the findings. Rigor Multiple strategies were used to ensure rigor. First, to ensure a representative sample, sampling strategies considered the participants’ age, sex, marital status, education, and transplant type. Second, to ensure credibility and reduce subjectivity, we used investigator triangulation, in which two researchers independently extracted themes during data analysis. Third, to conduct reliable research and ensure the validity of the results, all researchers received rigorous training in qualitative research methods through a program covering interviewing techniques, thematic analysis, and coding procedures. This provided them with the skills and knowledge necessary to conduct reliable research and ensure validity of the results. Finally, to enhance confirmability, researchers were actively engaged in self-reflection through team debriefings. Ethical considerations This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Fujian Medical University (IRB Ref No: 2023/83), and it adhered to the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided both verbal and written informed consent prior to participation. The participants volunteered their time and were not financially compensated for their participation. To ensure confidentiality, all data were anonymized and personal identifiers were removed from the transcripts. Results The interview transcripts presented in the results were translated by the bilingual research team. Characteristics of the participants A total of 23 patients were contacted for this study, of which 1 patient refused to be interviewed because of illness. Consequently, 22 patients were included in the final analysis. Interview duration averaged 23 min. The patients’ ages ranged from 18 to 56 years, with a median of 34.5 years. Other characteristics of the patients are summarized in Table . Fundamental themes Three themes and 11 subthemes reflecting the barriers to and the need for symptom self-management were observed among patients who underwent HSCT (Fig. ). These themes included limited awareness of symptom self-management, barriers to information acquisition, and multidimensional support needs. Theme 1: limited awareness of symptom self-management Subtheme 1: dependency Some patients exhibited a high level of dependency on symptom management. They expressed concerns about the potential risks of taking independent actions, fearing that incorrect self-management might worsen their condition. These patients often believe that guidance from HCPs is the only valid method to manage their symptoms, thereby neglecting the important role of self-management in the disease treatment process. “There’s no way to deal with it. I don’t know what there is to deal with. Tell the doctor that it’s best if I do whatever he tells me to do. Otherwise , it’s worse if I make a mistake.” (P15) . “If the doctor gives me medicine and tells me to take it , I take it; if he tells me to endure it , I endure it. I will do whatever the doctor says.” (P17) . In addition, some patients reported that family members played a protective role during the treatment process, aiming to reduce their psychological burden and decision-making responsibilities. However, this may limit the patients’ autonomy and sense of responsibility in self-management, further intensifying their reliance on others. “Well , I have sick so everything else is handled by my family… I don’t know much about my condition; it’s mostly my husband and my sister who talk to the doctor.” (P7) . “My family basically does all these things (related to the treatment of the disease) , so I don’t want to know any more about it. I just need to lie over here and cooperate with the treatment.” (P10) . Subtheme 2: passive suffering The symptoms experienced during HSCT, including nausea, vomiting, and fatigue, as well as practical issues, such as vascular access, have been shown to significantly deplete patients of energy and motivation. This physical challenges makes it difficult for patients to translate their self-management intentions into actions, thus resulting in a pattern of passive suffering where they endure the discomfort until it reaches an intolerable level. This phenomenon has been most frequently reported among patients undergoing high-intensity conditioning, reflecting their sense of helplessness and passivity in symptom self-management. “When I experience nausea and vomiting I usually tolerate it. For example , when I have diarrhea , the whole person will be more tired and I will have less appetite. In this case , I probably wouldn’t be able to get much help from the nurse. ” (P5) . “I tend to endure it if possible , but if I really can’t bear it anymore , there’s nothing I can do because I’ve

reaches an intolerable level. This phenomenon has been most frequently reported among patients undergoing high-intensity conditioning, reflecting their sense of helplessness and passivity in symptom self-management. “When I experience nausea and vomiting I usually tolerate it. For example , when I have diarrhea , the whole person will be more tired and I will have less appetite. In this case , I probably wouldn’t be able to get much help from the nurse. ” (P5) . “I tend to endure it if possible , but if I really can’t bear it anymore , there’s nothing I can do because I’ve already tried my best……I thought about exercising here , but I felt so exhausted that I decided against it. I might as well be a couch potato , since that was my initial plan—to do some radio calisthenics. After attempting just two sets , I found my hands and feet incredibly tired. I told myself , ‘Forget it , better be obedient and not engage in unauthorized activities.’” (P19) . Theme 2: information acquisition barriers Subtheme 1: lack of courage and skills in communication Due to the lack of knowledge and skills in symptom self-management, patients often rely on HCPs and their peers as their preferred sources of information. However, some patients lack the courage and skills to communicate, and they choose to avoid in-depth discussions with others for fear of increasing their psychological distress or receiving inappropriate advice. Patients also find it difficult to express their doubts to HCPs. These communication barriers limit the access to valuable information regarding symptom management and self-care. “Everyone has their own difficulties; asking too many questions might , in turn , cause others to feel psychologically uncomfortable , or perhaps they might find it hard to express themselves , right? So I seldom ask about these things.” (P6) . “One is the embarrassment of asking , for example , I feel the medical staff might think. Isn’t it just a fever? Just lie down quietly. I think that to myself and I’m too embarrassed to ask. I’m not sure if asking would even lead to a solution or anything. It’s just like that. The key is that I don’t know how to ask.” (P20) . Subtheme 2: clinician time constraints As the primary point of contact for patients in laminar airflow wards, HCPs perform essential medical procedures and provide daily care. Nevertheless, the consequences of understaffing and excessive workloads frequently manifest in suboptimal communication between HCPs and patients. Patient reports indicate that within laminar airflow environments, clinician time constraints significantly reduce opportunities for comprehensive patient-provider communication and delivering individualized care. This can result in patients’ information needs not being met. “I just feel that the doctors here are really too busy… Just these few doctors have to deal with so many of our patients.” (P6) . “I also wish the nurses could communicate with me more and teach me more. For example , how to prevent vomiting and how to deal with fatigue.” (P13) . Subtheme 3: overwhelming and diverse online information Patients generally lack a deep understanding of HSCT and attempt to find answers online. However, the vast amount of information available online, coupled with its variability, makes it difficult for patients to identify accurate, authoritative, and personally relevant information. This information overload increases patients’ anxiety and uncertainty, which affects their self-management of symptoms. “At present , I’m still in a state of confusion. I just search online for some fragmented information , which isn’t very accurate. I don’t know who to trust; there are various opinions and different perspectives.” (P11) These are all pretty much the same, just for reference, you can’t trust them completely. Theme 3: multidimensional support needs Subtheme 1: need for proactive symptom management Patients demonstrated strong concern about potential symptoms that may arise during transplantation (such as diarrhea and vomiting), expressing a desire to understand the causes of these symptoms and take self-management measures to prevent their occurrence. Some patients believe that preventing these symptoms is more important than treating them, particularly when the symptoms appear without a clear cause, which often leads to anxiety. “For example , when I have diarrhea , I just want to ask what I should do. I don’t know why I have diarrhea , because I usually eat normally , so of course I worry , why suddenly diarrhea?” (P3) . “Symptoms like vomiting , diarrhea , mouth ulcers—how to prevent them in advance , I think that’s more important , more important than treatment.” (P11) . “Also , generally when such things happen , the financial situation is often difficult , so I try to avoid it , like preventing infections , and also , if possible , it would be best if eating problems can be resolved.” (P1) .

I don’t know why I have diarrhea , because I usually eat normally , so of course I worry , why suddenly diarrhea?” (P3) . “Symptoms like vomiting , diarrhea , mouth ulcers—how to prevent them in advance , I think that’s more important , more important than treatment.” (P11) . “Also , generally when such things happen , the financial situation is often difficult , so I try to avoid it , like preventing infections , and also , if possible , it would be best if eating problems can be resolved.” (P1) . Subtheme 2: timely and effective symptom response need During HSCT, patients typically experience multiple symptoms of discomfort that affect their physical and mental states. Some patients mentioned taking certain self-management measures to cope with various symptoms during transplantation, but they found the effects unsatisfactory. “For vomiting , if you keep suppressing it , it won’t go away. You have to throw it all up , then it stops. Afterward , drinking a bit of water to cleanse the mouth is fine. Then , if you have an appetite , eat a little more , but if you don’t , just let it go; otherwise , vomiting is very uncomfortable.” (P19) . Therefore, the patients expressed a desire for more effective self-management strategies to relieve symptoms and reduce discomfort. “I want to know when symptoms like vomiting will ease a bit. When will the discomfort in my body subside?” (P13) . “I’m relying on my little bit of experience to stop vomiting , besides medication , and I’ll ask the nurse if there’s anything they can help me with. I also hope the nurse can communicate with me more and teach me more , like how to stop vomiting and how to deal with fatigue.” (P14) . Subtheme 3: internal support and self-regulation Many patients facing physical discomfort brought about by illness and treatment, experience psychological pressure and distress. However, only a small number of patients reported being able to independently adjust their mindsets and emotions, drawing on internal support to better manage symptoms and cope with challenges during treatment, thereby promoting recovery. “When I’m not feeling well , I just don’t want to talk , but everything else is fine. When I can’t eat , I get irritated and want to take it out on my family.” (P12) . “Illnesses need to be treated. Crying and complaining is also part of the treatment , and then we continue to cooperate; maybe the outcome will be better.” (P2) . “We need to regulate our mindset , face it bravely.” (A10) . Subtheme 4: longing for family and friends’ support and companionship During HSCT, the patients highly value the support and companionship of their families and friends. Through visits, emotional encouragement, and social support from loved ones, patients gain psychological comfort and strength, particularly when experiencing physical discomfort and fatigue. Additionally, concerns, words of consolation, and encouragement from friends contribute to providing comfort and emotional support and enhance their confidence in self-coping. “The greatest help from family members is to take care of the logistical support for us , such as preparing the three meals , and also providing some emotional comfort… Ideally , it would be great if the visit could happen , too. (Because) here (the patient points to the transparent visitation window in the room) , it was originally possible to visit , but I heard that later the visitation was stopped due to the COVID-19.” (P11). “Sometimes I tell my friends that I’m so tired , and they comfort me with a few words. Just hearing that makes me feel a bit more at ease.” (P19). Subtheme 5: peer support Peer support from fellow patients plays an important role in patient self-management. The shared identity as patients undergoing similar medical experiences creates a foundation of trust and mutual understanding, enabling the exchange of nuanced, practical knowledge that may not be covered in standardized patient education. The majority of patients expressed a desire to communicate with others who have similar experiences, hoping to exchange medical information, gain practical self-management strategies, and gain psychological comfort and strength. “I have a friend who just left here about a month and a half ago. I’ve talked to her a bit. I’ve also met some other patients at this hospital before. We’d all mention some things to pay attention to during our chats.” (P1) . “We encourage each other and share knowledge , such as how to deal with symptoms when they occur.” (P21). Subtheme 6: looking forward to an interactive information platform Patients expressed their anticipation of an interactive information platform that would enable them to conveniently access professional information. Additionally, they conveyed their preferences for the platform design. “It’s about the

friend who just left here about a month and a half ago. I’ve talked to her a bit. I’ve also met some other patients at this hospital before. We’d all mention some things to pay attention to during our chats.” (P1) . “We encourage each other and share knowledge , such as how to deal with symptoms when they occur.” (P21). Subtheme 6: looking forward to an interactive information platform Patients expressed their anticipation of an interactive information platform that would enable them to conveniently access professional information. Additionally, they conveyed their preferences for the platform design. “It’s about the different symptoms that appear at different stages , and then there will be a record like this. I think it’s quite good.” (P12). “Most nurses are female , while I am male. For instance , some (perianal care guidance) might be a bit inconvenient. It would be great if help could be provided online to solve the problem.” (P10). “For instance , for patients who have had treatment experiences within laminar airflow rooms before , if their messages , experiences or encouragement are left and seen by us , they should all be of some help to us.” (P13). Discussion This study aimed to explore the barriers and needs related to symptom self-management among patients in laminar airflow rooms who underwent HSCT. The findings indicate that patients with HSCT face diverse barriers to symptom self-management, including limited awareness, difficulty in obtaining information, and the need for multidimensional support. Effective self-management is crucial for improving treatment outcomes and recovery [ ]. However, we found that some patients exhibited limited awareness of symptom self-management and were highly dependent on HCPs and their families. This may stem from a subconscious perception of weakness, a medical culture that emphasizes professional authority over patient involvement and lack of self-management knowledge. Additionally, discomfort, limited social support, and poor communication with HCPs may contribute to this issue [ – ]. Pronounced reliance on family members can be understood as a manifestation of a paternalistic patient-family relationship, which is often influenced by cultural values that prioritize familial responsibility and authority. In such cultural contexts, family members are regarded as the primary decision-makers in healthcare. This relational dynamic can further diminish the patients’ awareness and motivation to engage in self-management [ , ]. We also found that the majority of patients opted to “endure” discomfort, a behavior potentially influenced by the cultural norm of “endurance” [ ]. In this context, minor ailments are often seen as challenges to be endured rather than actively addressed, which may limit the patients’ willingness to seek proactive solutions or engage in preventative care. Although some patients were aware of self-management, practical barriers hindered their effective use. Access to reliable scientific information is critical for symptom management, infection prevention, and quality of life improvement [ ]. Patients often turn to Baidu, RedNote, or Tiktok for related information, but the overload and variable quality of information make it difficult to identify trustworthy and helpful content. In addition, the busy schedules of HCPs and patients’ psychological concerns limit timely and effective guidance. The issue of the patients’ psychological concerns is congruent with the findings of Nickola et al. [ ]. In their study, an important aspect for patients with cancer was the fear of being refused, similar to that expressed by patients with HSCT in our study. Previous research has shown that self-management efficacy in patients with HSCT is negatively correlated with passive coping strategies. This finding indicates the need for enhanced self-management education to help patients develop proper awareness, increase their confidence in symptom self-management, and offer consistent and accessible support throughout the process [ , ]. This study showed that patients required multidimensional support within laminar airflow rooms, highlighting a strong desire for information on symptom self-management. Some patients expressed interest not only in learning how to manage symptoms but also in understanding their causes and receiving early prevention information. Most participants were particularly concerned with identifying effective self-coping strategies to alleviate their discomfort as quickly as possible. This aligns with the findings of Nguyen et al. [ ], who found that mastering the knowledge of symptoms and symptom relief skills can help patients overcome self-management difficulties and alleviate various symptoms. Furthermore, the fact that majority of the patients in this study wished to manage their symptoms with the help of an interactive information platform further demonstrated their quest for improved symptom self-management. These needs underscore the importance of a care approach that emphasizes the early identification, comprehensive assessment, and proactive management of distressing symptoms to alleviate suffering [ ]. Our findings also showed that social support, particularly from family and peers, plays a critical role in the emotional well-being of patients. Family support is especially crucial, as it provides both material and emotional

overcome self-management difficulties and alleviate various symptoms. Furthermore, the fact that majority of the patients in this study wished to manage their symptoms with the help of an interactive information platform further demonstrated their quest for improved symptom self-management. These needs underscore the importance of a care approach that emphasizes the early identification, comprehensive assessment, and proactive management of distressing symptoms to alleviate suffering [ ]. Our findings also showed that social support, particularly from family and peers, plays a critical role in the emotional well-being of patients. Family support is especially crucial, as it provides both material and emotional reassurance [ ]. One study demonstrated that patients undergoing HSCT who received strong family support showed better symptom management and faster recovery [ ]. However, the limitations of laminar airflow rooms, which restrict direct contact with family members, mean that patients should rely on digital forms of communication, such as video calls and text messages, to maintain these vital emotional connections. This is consistent with the cultural context in which families are seen as a primary source of emotional security, with patients frequently turning to family members for comfort. Additionally, peer support emerged as a significant need in our study, with patients recognizing its potential benefits, such as fostering emotional resonance and providing shared experiences that can reduce psychological distress and improve the overall quality of life [ , ]. Amonoo et al. [ ] also noted that, while opportunities for peer support may be limited, their importance is still acknowledged by patients. However, ensuring the quality and relevance of peer interactions remains challenging. Patients have raised concerns about the applicability of peer-sharing strategies, highlighting the risk that misinformation or poor communication may exacerbate the psychological burden [ ]. This concern underscores the importance of HCPs being vigilant in guiding peer interactions to avoid negative outcomes, as emphasized in previous research [ ]. In addition, some patients demonstrated self-regulation, drawing on internal strength to cope with the challenges of HSCT. Self-motivation, which includes traits, such as optimism and self-confidence, complements external support systems and is essential for navigating the challenges of HSCT treatment. The findings of Biagioli et al. [ ] support our observation, showing that patients who cultivate internal resilience mechanisms, such as optimism, experience better recovery and overall well-being. However, in our study, only a minority of participants reported being able to mobilize such internal resources effectively. The psychological distress problems of patients continue to persist [ ]. Individual’s social network plays a significant role in their mental health. This disparity between the potential benefit of self-regulation and patients’ frequent inability to utilize it indicates the importance of providing external psychosocial support for this group, rather than relying solely on the patients’ own coping abilities [ ]. To effectively address the multidimensional support needs of patients in symptom self-management, this study proposes the following solutions: (1) Enhanced Clinical Education Systems: Clinical nursing staff should prioritize enhancing symptom education, especially during critical phases such as the protective isolation period of HSCT, when the symptom burden is most severe. Comprehensive guidance on symptom self-management should be provided to empower patients to manage their symptoms effectively. (2) Social Support Optimization: Social support systems, including family members and peers, play a crucial role in helping patients build psychological resilience. Optimizing social support through training, assessment, and supervision can promote proactive coping strategies. Professional guidance should be provided when necessary to ensure that patients receive appropriate support. (3) Technology-enabled Support Platforms: The development of specialized online platforms that utilize mobile health technologies can offer patients a safe environment for receiving support and sharing information. These platforms would maximize emotional support, facilitate information exchange, and foster a sense of community. (4) Encouraging Positive Perspectives: Clinical interventions should focus on helping patients recognize the positive aspects of their lives. By guiding patients to identify the sources of hope and motivation, HCPs can enhance their confidence and drive them to manage their symptoms effectively. These strategies may help bridge the gap between current clinical practices and individualized needs of patients, thereby promoting better symptom management outcomes. Limitations Some limitations of the qualitative approach of this study should also be noted. First, the use of an interview guide may have influenced the final themes. Patients should have rather been allowed to speak freely without prompts. Second, although the participants in this study were from multiple provinces across the country, which enhanced the geographic diversity of the sample, the single-hospital setting limited the generalizability of the findings. Significant variations in healthcare resources, socioeconomic factors, and regional policies between provinces may have affected the broader applicability of our results. Finally, the study participants were all adults; therefore, the findings may not be applicable to children, adolescents, or the older population. Conclusions Despite the limitations, our qualitative study provides insights

Significant variations in healthcare resources, socioeconomic factors, and regional policies between provinces may have affected the broader applicability of our results.
